paper_metadata.title: The First Unprovoked Seizure in Typically Developing Children: A Real-Life Setting in Southern Brazil

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the setting, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and baseline characteristics. However, the use of a single tertiary center and the retrospective nature may introduce selection bias, as patients who did not have a second seizure might have been lost to follow-up or never referred to the specialized center.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: typically developing pediatric patients aged 28 days to 14 years who had a first unprovoked seizure at the Center of Pediatric Neurology of the Federal University of Paraná, Southern Brazil
items.reasoning: The authors clearly define the age range, developmental status, and geographic/institutional source.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: The medical records of 209 children were reviewed and a standardized protocol was used.
items.reasoning: While the review process is mentioned, the specific referral patterns to this tertiary center are not detailed, which could bias the sample toward more severe cases.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: This was a 10-year (between January 2006 and December 2016) retrospective study
items.reasoning: The dates are explicitly provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Center of Pediatric Neurology of the Federal University of Paraná, Southern Brazil, which is an academic and public tertiary hospital.
items.reasoning: The specific institution and its nature (public/academic/tertiary) are described.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Children with developmental delay, follow-up duration of less than 6 months, neonatal or provoked seizures, and a diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome were excluded.
items.reasoning: The criteria for exclusion are specific and align with the study's focus on 'typically developing' children.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: As a retrospective chart review, the 'participation rate' of all eligible children in the region is unknown; the study only includes those who reached the tertiary center.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The study protocol comprised the following variables: age at the first seizure, gender, sociodemographic data, pregnancy history, classification and duration of the first seizure...
items.reasoning: Table 1 and the text provide a comprehensive breakdown of the baseline clinical and demographic data.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study acknowledges a significant risk of attrition bias. Because it is retrospective, children who did not experience a second seizure may have been less likely to return for follow-up at a tertiary center, potentially inflating the recurrence rate (56.7%).

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: That possible bias can artificially increase the seizure recurrence rate observed in the present study.
items.reasoning: The authors admit that the retrospective design likely excluded patients who did not have a second seizure and were lost to follow-up.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no mention of attempting to contact families of children who did not return to the clinic.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: excluding patients who did not present with a second seizure and, therefore, lost follow-up.
items.reasoning: The authors hypothesize the reason for loss to follow-up but do not provide specific data on the number of patients lost or their reasons.

items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No data is provided comparing those who completed follow-up versus those who did not.

items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (EEG, age, seizure type) were measured using standardized clinical methods and ILAE definitions, which are reliable in a clinical setting.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: The EEG findings were categorized as (1) normal, (2) focal epileptic discharges, (3) generalized epileptic discharges...
items.reasoning: Prognostic factors like EEG and age groups are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: EEG was performed in every participant, as literature recommends.
items.reasoning: Standard clinical EEG and neuroimaging were used, which are the gold standards for these factors.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were divided into groups considering their age at the first seizure, as follows: (1) between 28 days and <1 year, (2) 1 to 3 years...
items.reasoning: Age categories are standard pediatric groupings and not seemingly derived from the data results.

items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All children were evaluated by a multiprofessional team... at the Center of Pediatric Neurology
items.reasoning: Measurements were conducted within a single specialized center using a standardized protocol.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: EEG was performed in every participant
items.reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (EEG) had 100% data availability.

items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Imputation was not mentioned; missing data (e.g., neuroimaging in 19%) was simply excluded from that specific analysis.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (seizure recurrence) is clearly defined using ILAE criteria. However, because it is a retrospective study, the timing and occurrence of recurrence rely on parental reporting and medical record documentation, which may be subject to recall bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Epilepsy was diagnosed when (1) 2 or more seizures occurred more than 24 hours apart...
items.reasoning: The study uses the standard ILAE definition for recurrence/epilepsy.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were followed-up every 3 to 6 months, or sooner if necessary, solely at clinic visits
items.reasoning: While clinical follow-up is standard, the retrospective nature means the 'measurement' of the outcome depends on whether the event was reported to the physician.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: evaluation by the entire multiprofessional team.
items.reasoning: All patients were followed at the same center by the same team.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study identifies several potential confounders but fails to use multivariable analysis to adjust for them. The reported associations (e.g., age < 5 years) are based on univariable tests, which cannot account for the influence of other variables.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: The study protocol comprised the following variables: age... gender... treatment with antiepileptic drugs, etiology and recurrence.
items.reasoning: The authors collected data on most standard confounders in epilepsy studies.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: treatment with antiepileptic drugs... carbamazepine was the most used (32.4%)
items.reasoning: While drugs are named, specific dosages or durations of treatment (which could confound recurrence) are not detailed.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: retrospective study based on medical records, which may alter the results found, especially due to lack of data.
items.reasoning: The reliability of confounder measurement is limited by the retrospective nature of the chart review.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: standardized protocol was used.
items.reasoning: A single protocol was applied to all record reviews.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation methods were described.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: strict inclusion and exclusion criteria were used, in order to homogenize the group
items.reasoning: The study used restriction (typically developing children only) to control for neurodevelopmental status as a confounder.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: The variables were analyzed using Student's t test, Fisher's exact test, and Pearson correlation.
items.reasoning: The authors only used univariable statistical tests. No multivariable regression (e.g., Cox or Logistic) was performed to adjust for confounding.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The analysis is straightforward but limited. The lack of multivariable modeling and survival analysis (e.g., Kaplan-Meier) for time-to-event data is a significant methodological weakness for a prognosis study.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: The variables were analyzed using Student's t test, Fisher's exact test, and Pearson correlation.
items.reasoning: The strategy is clearly stated, even if it is basic.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There was no multivariable model building described.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: The level of statistical significance was established at P < .05.
items.reasoning: While the tests used are correct for simple associations, they are insufficient for a prognostic study which should ideally account for follow-up time and multiple predictors.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: There was no statistically significant association between seizure recurrence and follow-up period, treatment... EEG or neuroimaging findings (P > .05).
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings transparently.
